title_clean: Nifty at 20,000: techno-fundamental case and a put calendar
summary: Builds a case for Nifty 20,000 in 3-4 months (heavyweight catch-up, rolling-return mean reversion, supertrend 21/53 trend-persistence) and demonstrates a deep-ITM put calendar as a low-margin bullish alternative to naked put selling, with roll costs as the defined monthly risk.
lessons: Two supertrend lines (20-day/5-day) proxy monthly and weekly trends; alignment defines regime.
Trends historically persisted 10-12 weeks; extensions beyond that signaled outsized continuation rallies (post-COVID, post-inflation).
A deep-ITM put calendar converts a bullish view into low-margin, capped-risk exposure; roll-over cost (~₹3,500-4,000/month) is the real max risk.
Effective margin = gross margin minus next-day premium credit - check net, not gross, returns.

title_clean: The reality of intraday trading: costs, taxes and the 9:20 straddle
summary: Anatomy of the popular 9:20 short straddle (sideways/trending/choppy outcomes), then a full cost audit of intraday option selling: ~₹230/day charges on a 2-lot hedged Bank Nifty straddle (~₹57,000/yr ≈ 65% of capital), MTM-vs-net-profit illusion, and intraday's 'speculative income' tax treatment with no expense deduction.
lessons: Backtests that ignore charges and slippage overstate returns; real costs can consume most of a small account's capital.
Stamp duty is paid on both sides; with STT, brokerage and GST, costs compound daily - annualize them before believing any strategy.
MTM screenshots show gross P&L: a claimed 1% day can be ~0.5% net after ~₹230 of charges on ₹45,000 capital.
Tax treatment matters more than strategy edge for high-frequency trading; check the income classification before scaling up.
Choppy markets defeat straddle stop-loss logic on both sides - the regime, not the entry time, decides the outcome.

title_clean: Low-VIX regime strategy: buy-and-sell combo with margin optimization

lessons: In very low VIX never run pure naked shorts - pair buys with sells so a VIX spike cushions both sides.
Strangle sellers get trapped when the market just touches resistance: panic exit at the top, then fear re-entry lower.
Anchor ratio legs to real support/resistance (18,900 support / 20,000 resistance), not arbitrary strikes.
Margin netting: a sold call against a sold put zeroes the span component - optimize capital by netting naked legs.
Lower breakeven = support minus net premium collected; here 18,962 vs the 18,900 support.

title_clean: Long-term ratio spreads for a mildly bearish market
summary: Designs long-dated (December) ratio structures for a slightly bearish view: buy 21,000PE, sell 3× 19,000PE, sell 2× 21,000CE (breakevens ~18,000/21,000, ~40% max profit, ~4%/month expected), plus the bullish mirror (1:4 call ratio with credit-fixing adjustments) and the combined non-directional version.
lessons: For a mildly directional multi-month view, deep-ITM long leg financed by ratio shorts beats naked option selling on margin and risk.
Equalize or over-cover naked legs with opposite-side shorts to shrink margin; add wings if unlimited risk is unacceptable.
Aim for ~4%/month on deployed capital - consistent with the ~30-40% p.a. realism ceiling.
Combine a call ratio and put ratio for a non-directional structure; book whichever leg is winning when the market stretches.
Credit-fixing: adjust leg counts (sell fewer far puts, one nearer put) to flip a net-debit structure to net credit.
